title: How to Read a Research Article
text:
Academic articles are written to communicate original research to a specialized audience, so they follow a predictable structure. Readers rarely need to proceed linearly; many experienced scholars begin with the abstract to decide whether the study is relevant before examining the methodology in detail. The introduction typically establishes a gap in existing knowledge and states the hypothesis the study tests. Careful readers therefore treat the article as an argument that must be evaluated rather than a set of facts to be accepted.

Evaluating an article also requires attention to what it does not say. Limitations are often tucked into the final section, yet they indicate how far the findings can reasonably be generalized. Similarly, the citation list reveals whose work the authors consider foundational, which can expose the intellectual tradition they are working within. A critical reader who notices these signals is better placed to judge whether the conclusions are warranted by the evidence.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what does the introduction typically establish?
options: A gap in existing knowledge and the hypothesis
A list of the author's previous publications

questions.text: According to the second paragraph, where are limitations often found?
What does the passage imply about how experienced scholars read academic articles?
options: They do not always read the article in order
They rely only on the citation list

questions.text: What can be inferred about the purpose of noticing limitations and citations?
options: It helps readers judge how far the conclusions are supported
It allows readers to find the author's contact details
It replaces the need to read the methodology
It shows which journal published the study

vocabulary.definition: a statement that a study tests to see whether it is true
weaknesses or restrictions that reduce how far results can be applied
a reference to another source of information
applied more broadly to other cases or situations

paragraph_translations: Los artículos académicos se escriben para comunicar investigaciones originales a un público especializado, por lo que siguen una estructura predecible. Los lectores rara vez necesitan avanzar de forma lineal; muchos investigadores experimentados comienzan por el resumen para decidir si el estudio es relevante antes de examinar la metodología en detalle. La introducción suele establecer un vacío en el conocimiento existente y plantear la hipótesis que el estudio pone a prueba. Por ello, los lectores atentos tratan el artículo como un argumento que debe evaluarse, y no como un conjunto de hechos que deba aceptarse sin más.

Evaluar un artículo también exige prestar atención a lo que no dice. Las limitaciones suelen ocultarse en la sección final, pero indican hasta qué punto los resultados pueden generalizarse con razón. De igual modo, la lista de citas revela qué trabajos consideran fundamentales los autores, lo que puede mostrar la tradición intelectual en la que se inscriben. Un lector crítico que advierte estas señales está mejor preparado para juzgar si las conclusiones están justificadas por la evidencia.
